Headache Pharmacology

Classifying migraine, cluster, and tension headache from clinical presentation, then matching abortive and preventive therapy to the diagnosis — plus the trap that connects all three: medication overuse headache.

Headache

Classification, Epidemiology & Red Flags

Headache is one of the most common complaints in medicine — nearly everyone will have one. The clinical job is sorting the overwhelming majority of benign, predictable primary headaches from the rare but dangerous secondary headaches that signal something else is going on.

Epidemiology

📊

90%

of patients will experience a headache in their lifetime

🧒

75%

of pediatric patients have had a headache by age 15

💰

$27 Billion/yr

cost associated with migraine alone (medical care + lost work hours)

🧬

4×

risk of a primary headache disorder if a first-degree relative has one — and the type tends to run true

Pathophysiology

  • Headache pain initiates in the trigeminal afferents that innervate blood vessels, mucosa, and muscles
  • Secondary headaches stimulate this pathway via inflammation and/or compression from an underlying cause
  • Primary headache disorders occur spontaneously via chemical mediators such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) — the target of an entire modern drug class you'll see repeatedly in this lecture
☐ When to Look Deeper — Secondary Headache Red Flags
  • New onset at an older age, without prior history or a positive family history
  • Unexplained, abnormal worsening of a previously stable migraine pattern
  • Dramatic or unusual change in the character of the prodrome or the headache itself
  • Headache that wakes the patient at night (except cluster headache, which does this routinely)
  • Much worse when recumbent, only when upright, or with coughing/sneezing/Valsalva
  • "Worst headache of my life" — sudden, unusually severe onset
  • Focal neurologic deficits that persist after the headache resolves
  • Any abnormal neurologic or new psychiatric finding on exam
  • New headache in a patient with HIV, malignancy, or pregnancy

Source: Goldman-Cecil Medicine, 2024. Primary headaches are notably repeatable and predictable — they vary little in intensity, location, or character between episodes. It's a change from that stable pattern that should raise concern.

History Taking

  1. Family historyHelps establish baseline risk and expected headache type.
  2. Patient's lifetime headache historyNew? Increasing in frequency? Longstanding but finally bothersome enough to seek care?
  3. Current headache — "tell me about it"Unilateral or bilateral? Quality (stabbing, pounding, tight)? Positional or Valsalva-related?
  4. Medical and psychiatric history
  5. Medication useSome drugs cause headache directly; frequent analgesic use specifically can cause medication overuse headache — a recurring theme in this lecture.

Treatment — The 30,000-Foot View

  • Treatment depends on headache type and severity
  • Mild headaches are often treated with an NSAID, acetaminophen, or a combination OTC formulation (many contain caffeine) — patients frequently self-treat before ever seeking care
✅ Supportive measures — helpful for every headache type

Rest in a quiet, dark room · cold compress over the eyes · hot shower · massage · biofeedback training (patients learn to control involuntary physiologic processes) · osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT)

Primary Headache Types at a Glance

Pain distribution by headache type — location and pattern are among the most useful clinical clues

Migraine

Unilateral, throbbing/pounding — the "5-4-3-2-1" pattern.

Cluster Headache

Excruciating periorbital, stabbing pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs.

Tension Headache

Bilateral, band-like, steady pressure — the most common primary headache.

Sinus headache is technically a secondary headache — inflammation from allergy or infection compressing the trigeminal nerve. Treating the underlying sinus process resolves it, which is why it isn't grouped with the primary headache disorders.

Q: A 45-year-old with a 10-year history of stable migraines describes their current headache as "the worst headache of my life," with a much more sudden onset than usual. What should this trigger?

Answer

This is a secondary headache red flag despite the migraine history — sudden, unusually severe onset ("worst headache of my life") and a dramatic change in character from the patient's normal stable pattern both warrant looking deeper (e.g., for subarachnoid hemorrhage) rather than assuming "just another migraine."

Primary Headaches

Migraine

Characteristics — The "5-4-3-2-1" Rule

🔑 5-4-3-2-1
  • 5 or more attacks
  • 4 hours to 3 days duration, untreated
  • 2 or more of: unilateral · throbbing/pounding · moderate-severe pain · worsened by activity
  • 1 of: nausea/vomiting or photo-/phonophobia

The buzzword to listen for: unilateral throbbing or pounding pain.

  • Thought to arise from irritation of CN V, the meninges, or blood vessels via release of substance P and other vasoactive peptides → vasodilation
  • ~3:1 female:male predominance
  • Triggers: caffeine, excessive sleep, alcohol, certain foods, emotional stress, menstrual cycle

Aura

Temporary neurologic symptoms preceding or coinciding with the start of the headache:

Visual (most common)

Zig-zag lines, shimmering, flashing lights, or blind spots — a scintillating scotoma that often expands across the visual field.

Sensory

Paresthesia that can travel/march across a body region.

Speech & Language

Difficulty speaking, mumbling, or dysphasia.

Visual aura — the most common aura type, often described as a shimmering, zigzag pattern that progresses across the visual field

Acute (Abortive) Treatment

Milder Migraine

Non-specific analgesics: NSAID, acetaminophen, or combination formulations (APAP/aspirin/caffeine). Patients often self-treat with these before ever being diagnosed.

Moderate-to-Severe

Triptans (gold standard), ergotamines, or CGRP receptor antagonists ("gepants"). Most patients seeking care for migraine are not mild cases.

Triptans — Selective 5-HT1B/5-HT1D Agonists

  • Act on cranial arteries as vasoconstrictors, decreasing the hyper-vasodilation thought to underpin migraine pathology
  • Inhibit trigeminal nerve activity, preventing vasoactive peptide release
  • 80% of patients experience symptom relief within 2 hours; 24-hour recurrence drops to roughly 20–40%
  • All triptans share similar efficacy — they differ mainly in pharmacokinetic profile (onset, half-life, route, metabolism)
DrugRelative OnsetHalf-LifeNotable PK Feature
SumatriptanFastShort (~2.5 h)PO, SC, and intranasal forms; also used for cluster headache
RizatriptanFastShort (~2–3 h)Orally disintegrating tablet available
ZolmitriptanFastShortPO and intranasal; nasal spray also used for cluster headache
AlmotriptanIntermediateIntermediatePartly metabolized via CYP3A4 and MAO
EletriptanIntermediateIntermediateMetabolized via CYP3A4 — avoid strong 3A4 inhibitors
NaratriptanSlowLong (~6 h)Better tolerability, slower onset
FrovatriptanSlowestLongest (~26 h)Lowest recurrence rate

FYI-level detail — not for memorizing exact numbers. The concept that matters: longer half-life → slower onset but longer duration/lower recurrence, and vice versa.

⚠️ Triptans — AEs, Contraindications, DDIs

AEs: paresthesia, dizziness, warm/hot sensation, and — the big one — chest discomfort/pressure/tightness (the vasoconstrictive effect occurring in the wrong tissue). Contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension. DDIs: CYP3A4 involvement for eletriptan and almotriptan; theoretical serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs (in practice, less of a hard contraindication than the warning label suggests).

Ergots — Ergotamine & Dihydroergotamine

Non-Specific Serotonin Agonists

Act on 5-HT receptors to vasoconstrict, similar to triptans, and also act as partial agonists at α-adrenergic receptors — a less selective mechanism. Ergot alkaloids are produced by Claviceps purpurea, a fungus that infects grasses and grains (especially rye) under damp conditions — the same class of compound responsible for historical ergotism outbreaks (muscle spasms, hallucinations, gangrene from vasospasm).

  • AEs similar to triptans, plus prominent nausea/vomiting — pretreat with the dopaminergic antiemetic metoclopramide (preferred over serotonergic antiemetics, to avoid compounding serotonin syndrome risk)
  • Adverse effect burden plus the rise of CGRP antagonists has limited the clinical utility of ergots — still available and indicated, but less commonly used

Gepants — CGRP Receptor Antagonists

  • Block CGRP from binding its receptor, decreasing the action of this key signaling mediator in migraine pathology (a potent vasodilator on cranial vasculature and the trigeminal ganglion) — reduces neurogenic pain signaling and inflammation (↓ neurokinin A and substance P)
  • Acute (abortive): ubrogepant, rimegepant
  • Preventive: rimegepant (dual-use), atogepant
✅ The cardiovascular-disease answer

Unlike triptans and ergots, CGRP antagonists are not vasoconstrictors and can be used in patients with cardiovascular disease — this is the single most important clinical differentiator to remember. (Emerging literature suggests uncontrolled hypertension may be worth watching, but this hasn't yet changed treatment algorithms.)

⚠️ Gepants — AEs, CIs, DDIs

AEs: constipation, nausea, somnolence, and new-onset or exacerbated Raynaud's phenomenon (in one study of 169 Raynaud's patients on a CGRP antagonist, 9 developed microvascular complications, 2 severe — including digital autonecrosis; counsel patients to report new cold sensitivity or tingling). CIs: severe liver or kidney disease, hypersensitivity. DDIs: pharmacokinetic interactions via CYP3A4 and drug transporters (P-gp, organic anion transporters).

Preventive Treatment

🔑 When to start prophylaxis

Recommended when headaches interfere with daily activities 3 or more times a month (still episodic migraine — not yet chronic).

Beta Blockers

Propranolol — first-line

Cheap and effective in most patients — the default starting point before escalating to more expensive options.

CGRP Antibodies / Inhibitors

First-line alongside beta blockers

Highly effective — reserved for escalation in practice mainly due to cost, not efficacy concerns.

Calcium Channel Blocker

Verapamil — off-label

Non-dihydropyridine CCB; effective for migraine prevention despite lacking an FDA-approved indication for it.

TCA

Amitriptyline

Broad receptor activity (SERT/NET inhibition plus multiple other targets) — same drug covered for neuropathic pain and tension headache prevention.

Anticonvulsants

Valproate, Topiramate

Name-recognition level for this course — mechanism and AEs covered in the anticonvulsants lecture.

OnabotulinumtoxinA

Chronic migraine only

Extremely effective specifically for chronic migraine — see below.

CGRP Antibodies (Preventive)

DrugTarget
ErenumabExtracellular domain of the CGRP receptor itself
EptinezumabCGRP (the signaling peptide)
FremanezumabCGRP (the signaling peptide)
GalcanezumabCGRP (the signaling peptide)
  • Effective with a good safety and tolerability profile; administered subcutaneously
  • Expensive: roughly $10,000–$20,000/year depending on drug and source — the main practical barrier to first-line use
  • The erenumab autoinjector contains dry natural rubber — caution with latex allergy

OnabotulinumtoxinA — Chronic Migraine Preventive

💡 Mechanism

Cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing vesicular fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles to the presynaptic terminal membrane — blocking ACh release and producing localized muscle paralysis. Indicated specifically for chronic migraine (≥8 migraine days/month for ≥3 months).

OnabotulinumtoxinA injection sites for chronic migraine (source: migrainecanada.org) — exact sites are not required memorization for this course

Signs of response: decreased migraine intensity, improved response to abortive medications, improved tolerance of known triggers, reduced neck pain, and decreased associated symptoms (e.g. nausea).

Migraine treatment summary — acute vs. preventive options mapped against severity and cardiovascular risk

Q: A patient with a history of Prinzmetal (vasospastic) angina needs an abortive medication for a moderate-severe migraine. What's the gold-standard answer here — and why not the usual gold standard?

Answer

A CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant), not a triptan. Triptans and ergots are vasoconstrictors and are contraindicated in cardiovascular disease, including vasospastic angina. CGRP antagonists work by a different mechanism and are safe to use in patients with cardiovascular disease.

Primary Headaches

Cluster Headache

Characteristics

  • Excruciating periorbital pain with autonomic symptoms — stabbing or boring pain, often described as a "hot poker" behind the eye
  • Ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, ptosis/miosis, and eyelid swelling — all on the same side as the pain
  • Patients are restless — pacing or rocking (a sharp contrast to migraine, where patients want to stay still in a dark room)
  • Attacks occur in clusters: daily to multiple times a day, for days to weeks at a time; each individual attack lasts 15 minutes to 3 hours
🔑 Migraine vs. cluster — behavior during an attack

Migraine: patient wants to lie still in a quiet, dark room. Cluster: patient is restless, pacing, or rocking. This behavioral difference alone can help distinguish the two at the bedside, on top of the unilateral-throbbing vs. periorbital-stabbing pain quality.

  • More common in males, roughly 3:1 to as high as 6–7:1 depending on the source
  • Attacks typically begin between ages 20 and 30
  • Can be precipitated by alcohol, histamine, or nitroglycerin
  • High correlation with suicidal ideation and behaviors, reflecting the severity of the pain — this history is clinically important to screen for in these patients
💡 The key differentiator: NSAID non-response

Cluster headaches do not respond to NSAIDs — this is the single biggest distinguishing feature from other similarly-presenting boring/stabbing periorbital headaches (e.g. paroxysmal hemicrania, which does respond to NSAIDs — indomethacin is the classic answer for an NSAID-responsive boring headache that isn't a cluster headache).

Acute Treatment

  1. 100% oxygen8–10 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 10–15 minutes. Outcomes are not improved by extending beyond 15 minutes.
  2. Sumatriptan (oral or SC) or zolmitriptan (nasal spray)Same triptan class used for migraine.
  3. VerapamilCan also be used for prophylaxis — one prescription covers both acute and preventive needs.

Preventive Treatment

Verapamil — Drug of Choice

Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; mechanism not fully understood but effective. Often dosed for the duration of a predictable cluster period (some are seasonal) rather than continuously year-round.

Lithium — Alternative

Second-line option; carries its own adverse effect profile (covered in more detail in psychiatry pharmacology).

Patients with predictable cluster periods (seasonal or trigger-based) often keep a headache journal, which helps identify when to start and stop preventive verapamil rather than dosing it continuously.

Q: A patient describes nightly episodes of severe, stabbing pain behind one eye lasting under an hour, with tearing and eyelid drooping on the same side. NSAIDs haven't touched it. What's the diagnosis, and what's your first move?

Answer

Cluster headache. First-line acute treatment is 100% oxygen at 8–10 L/min via non-rebreather for 10–15 minutes. If that fails, sumatriptan or zolmitriptan nasal spray are next, and verapamil can cover both abortive and preventive needs.

Primary Headaches

Tension Headache

Characteristics

  • The most common type of primary headache
  • Episodic, often associated with a stressor (work, a big exam, a life event)
  • Bilateral, band-like pain — the classic buzzword is a "band wrapped around my head"
  • Steady, non-pulsatile pain — no aura, no nausea
  • Can present with photophobia or phonophobia, but never both together (this is what separates it from migraine)
  • Duration 4–6 hours untreated, though it can be constant
  • Also described as a "holocranial headache without nausea or vomiting"
  • Slightly more common in females; classified as episodic (<15 headache days/month) or chronic (>15 headache days/month)

Tension headache — bilateral, band-like pain distribution

🔑 The only bilateral primary headache

Of the three primary headache types covered in this lecture, tension headache is the only one that's classically bilateral. Migraine is unilateral; cluster headache is unilateral/periorbital. Bilateral, band-like pain should point you toward tension headache first.

Acute Treatment

Episodic tension-type headaches generally respond well to:

AgentTypical Dose Range
Acetaminophen650–1000 mg
Aspirin250–1000 mg
Naproxen250–500 mg
Ibuprofen200–800 mg
Ketoprofen12.5–75 mg
⚠️ The 3-day trap

Analgesic use for more than 3 days per week can worsen headaches and lead to medication-induced headache. Given that chronic tension headache is defined as >15 headache days/month, it's easy to see how a patient reaching for an NSAID or APAP that often could tip into this cycle — a direct segue into medication overuse headache, covered next. NSAID mechanism is also a reminder here: nonselective COX inhibition reduces the prostaglandins that normally protect gastric mucosa, so frequent NSAID use also raises ulcer risk independent of the headache-worsening effect.

Preventive Treatment

Chronic tension-type headache may benefit from prophylaxis:

Amitriptyline

Start at 10 mg at bedtime, increasing slowly up to 100 mg until the patient improves or intolerable side effects develop. Same drug used for migraine prevention and neuropathic pain — same broad receptor-activity profile applies.

Also consider: biofeedback, cognitive behavioral therapy, stress management, osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT), physical therapy, and acupuncture — all endorsed by the headache literature as adjuncts or alternatives to pharmacotherapy.

Q: A patient with chronic tension headache (18 headache days/month) has been using ibuprofen almost daily to cope. What two problems does this create, independent of each other?

Answer

First, the pharmacologic AE risk of frequent NSAID use — GI ulceration, since COX inhibition reduces the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Second, and specific to headache management, analgesic use >3 days/week risks medication overuse headache, which will worsen the underlying problem it's meant to treat. The correct move here is starting a preventive agent (amitriptyline) rather than continuing to escalate the as-needed NSAID.

Headache

Medication Overuse Headache

The trap that connects migraine, tension headache, and (to a lesser extent) cluster headache: the very drugs used to abort an attack can, with frequent use, become the cause of more frequent and more severe headaches.

⚠️ What causes it

Overuse of acute/abortive drugs — especially butalbital and opioids, but also triptans, NSAIDs, ergots, and (formerly) lasmiditan — leads to increased frequency and severity of headache with poor response to both acute and preventive treatment.

The Vicious Cycle

  1. Take the abortive drugSumatriptan (or another abortive) relieves the current headache.
  2. Drug wears offA rebound headache develops as the drug is withdrawn from the system — this is not exclusive to headache medications (compare rebound congestion with nasal decongestants).
  3. Take another doseThe patient treats the rebound headache with another dose of the same abortive.
  4. Repeat, worsening each timeEach subsequent cycle tends to produce a worse headache, and the pattern becomes self-sustaining — daily or near-daily headache with heavy abortive use is the hallmark presentation.

Treatment

  • Withdraw the overused drug(s) — abrupt withdrawal may require hospitalization and bridge therapy with other drugs
  • Consider starting preventive treatment for the underlying headache disorder
  • Goal: limit future acute treatment to no more than 2 days per week
  • Taper, don't stop cold turkey — going from daily use straight to twice-weekly is unrealistic and will provoke severe rebound; titrate down gradually
✅ CGRP antagonists — the preferred switch target

CGRP receptor antagonists have not been associated with development of medication overuse headache, unlike triptans, NSAIDs, ergots, opioids, and butalbital. When cost isn't prohibitive, tapering the overused abortive while transitioning the patient to a CGRP antagonist is often the preferred course — treating the acute headaches effectively without perpetuating the overuse cycle.

🔑 Lasmiditan — a name you may still see in board prep

Lasmiditan (a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist) was discontinued in Fall 2025, with existing U.S. supply expected to run out by June 2026. You may still encounter it in board-prep materials, but it should be phasing out of both clinical practice and current board content given it's no longer available to prescribe.

Q: A patient with migraine has been using sumatriptan roughly 20 days a month because their headache returns as soon as the drug wears off. What's happening, and what's the best next step?

Answer

This is medication overuse headache. The best next step is to taper the sumatriptan (not stop abruptly) while transitioning to a CGRP antagonist, which isn't associated with rebound/overuse headache. If a CGRP antagonist isn't accessible, taper the sumatriptan down toward a goal of no more than 2 days/week of use.

🔑 Mnemonic recap
  • 5-4-3-2-1, unilateral pounding → migraine
  • Banded → tension headache
  • Ice pick / boring, NSAID non-responsive → cluster headache
  • Daily headache with heavy abortive use → medication overuse headache
  • Electrified toothbrush (brief, triggered, stabbing facial pain) → trigeminal neuralgia (bonus disease index — see case below)

Case Practice

These mirror the format used in lecture — work through the diagnosis before checking the answer.

Case 1: A 34-year-old woman reports recurrent headaches several times a month, "usually when things at work really pick up." Dull, bilateral pressure lasting several hours, not associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or worsening with exercise. What type of headache, and how would you manage it?

Answer

Tension headache — bilateral, stress-associated, band-like/pressure quality, no nausea or exercise-related worsening. Manage acutely with NSAIDs or acetaminophen, plus non-pharmacologic measures (OMT, biofeedback, stress management). Ask about frequency — if ≥15 headache days/month, add a preventive (amitriptyline).

Case 2: A 26-year-old woman has had recurrent headaches for 3 years, roughly twice a month. They begin with flashing zigzag lights in her left visual field, followed 20 minutes later by severe right-sided throbbing pain lasting ~12 hours, with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. She's currently having an attack. What's the most appropriate medication to administer right now?

Answer

Migraine with aura. For an active attack, a triptan is the abortive answer as written (no cardiovascular history given — don't assume one that isn't stated). In real practice you'd confirm cardiovascular history first; if present, a CGRP antagonist would be the safer abortive choice instead.

Case 3: A 61-year-old has sudden episodes of severe stabbing pain in the right cheek and jaw, each lasting only seconds, triggered by brushing their teeth or lightly touching the face. Neuro exam is normal. Most appropriate medication?

Answer

Trigeminal neuralgia — brief, trigger-evoked, electric/stabbing facial pain ("electrified toothbrush"). Not technically one of the three primary headaches covered here, but it's fair game given the shared trigeminal-nerve theme. First-line agent: carbamazepine (sodium channel blocker, also a CYP3A4 inducer) — the same drug covered as DOC for trigeminal neuralgia in the pain pharmacology material.

Case 4: A 38-year-old with longstanding migraine has developed near-daily headaches over the past 6 months, taking sumatriptan roughly 20 days each month because the headache recurs as the drug wears off. Neuro exam normal. Most appropriate next step?

Answer

Medication overuse headache. Taper the sumatriptan and transition to a CGRP antagonist if accessible. If not, taper toward a goal of ≤2 days/week of abortive use.

Case 5: A 42-year-old man has excruciating headaches nightly for 3 weeks. Each begins suddenly, lasts ~45 minutes, centered behind his left eye. He becomes extremely restless during attacks, with non-stop tearing and eyelid drooping on the left side. Neuro exam normal. What intervention should be used to abort the headache?

Answer

Cluster headache. First-line abortive: 100% oxygen, 8–10 L/min via non-rebreather for 10–15 minutes. NSAIDs will not work. If oxygen is insufficient, sumatriptan or zolmitriptan nasal spray, or verapamil (which doubles as prevention for his likely recurring cluster period).

Q: Across all the headache types in this lecture, what's the one management principle that applies universally regardless of diagnosis?

Answer

Watch the frequency of abortive/analgesic use. Any headache type treated with as-needed medication more than roughly 2–3 days per week risks tipping into medication overuse headache — the diagnosis and the drug class may differ, but this trap is the same across migraine, tension headache, and (to a lesser extent) cluster headache.
